name: Black seed oil hair
lead: Black seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Nigella sativa, an annual flowering plant also called black cumin, kalonji or nigella. It is used in looksmaxxing and hair-care circles as a scalp oil and as an oral supplement by people who want thicker-looking hair or who are trying to slow shedding [1]. Its best-known aromatic constituent is thymoquinone [1][2].

People who use it for hair typically apply it to the scalp as part of an oiling routine, mix it into carrier oils or shampoos, or take it as capsules alongside other hair supplements. Proponents describe the oil as nourishing for the scalp and say regular use helps hair look fuller and healthier. These are community beliefs rather than findings from hair trials.

Hair-specific human research is small. A 2013 double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study of 20 women with acute telogen effluvium tested a daily scalp lotion containing 0.5% Nigella sativa oil and reported higher hair density and thickness after three months than placebo. [18] A company-reported 28-day study of a 5% black-seed-oil scalp lotion in 22 adults has also been publicised. [19] Published and registered clinical research on the oil otherwise concerns other conditions, such as osteoarthritis, asthma, diabetes and hypertension, and Wikipedia notes that high-quality clinical evidence for treating human disease with the seeds or oil is limited [1][3][4][5][6].

angle.text: Users apply black seed oil to the scalp or take it as capsules in the hope of thicker, healthier-looking hair and less shedding. The route from the oil to visible hair change is described by proponents through scalp nourishment and thymoquinone's anti-inflammatory activity.

paras: Nigella sativa is native to western Asia and eastern Europe and is naturalised across parts of Europe, North Africa and east to Myanmar. It grows 20 to 30 cm tall with pale blue and white flowers, and the seeds are used as a spice in breads, curries and spice mixes such as panch phoron [1].

The seed oil makes up roughly a third to two fifths of the seed by weight. It contains fatty acids such as linoleic, oleic and palmitic acid, along with aromatic compounds including thymoquinone, dihydrothymoquinone, p-cymene, carvacrol and thymol [1].

Nigella sativa is an annual flowering plant of the buttercup family, 20 to 30 cm tall, with finely divided leaves and pale blue or white flowers; its capsules hold the black seeds from which the oil is pressed. Common names include black cumin, black caraway, nigella and kalonji. [1]

The oil makes up roughly a third of the seed and contains linoleic, oleic and palmitic acids together with aromatic compounds including thymoquinone, the constituent most often named in marketing and research. [1][16] The seeds are also a kitchen spice, used dry-roasted in curries and in the Bengali panch phoron blend, and the US FDA classes them as generally recognized as safe for use as a spice or flavouring. [1]

In hair-care communities the oil is used topically (massaged into the scalp, sometimes warmed or diluted with a carrier oil) and orally (as softgels or liquid). Users discuss it alongside other natural options for thinning hair, and often as a complement to routines built around minoxidil or finasteride.

Supporters point to thymoquinone's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties in laboratory studies as a rationale for scalp use [2][7]. Those laboratory studies concern cancer cells, immune signalling and oxidative stress rather than hair follicles.

Preparations in the telogen effluvium pilot study and the company-reported study were scalp lotions applied daily, while community routines more often involve warmed oil massaged in and left on before washing. [18][19]

Archaeological evidence shows cultivation of the plant for about three millennia, with seeds recovered from several ancient Egyptian sites, including the tomb of Tutankhamun, and from a Hittite flask in Turkey [1]. The Persian physician Avicenna described the seeds in The Canon of Medicine, and the plant has a long place in traditional medicine in Western Asia, North Africa and South Asia [1][2].

A 2008 review surveyed the traditional uses and pharmacology of the seeds, and a 2017 review describes their place in prophetic medicine traditions, where the seeds are recommended for many complaints [2][8].

Seeds have been found in ancient Egyptian contexts, including Tutankhamun's tomb, and the plant has a long record in the traditional medicine of Western Asia; Avicenna described its use for breathing difficulty. [1][2] A review of the plant in the 'Prophetic medicine' tradition documents its place in Islamic traditional practice. [8]

This heritage is a large part of how the oil is presented to hair-care audiences: proponents describe it as a traditional remedy applied to the scalp or taken by mouth, and the claims of thickening, shedding reduction and shine are made on that basis. Wikipedia notes that there is insufficient high-quality clinical evidence that the seeds or oil treat human disease, with weak evidence of short-term blood pressure reduction and possible small changes in blood lipids in some reviews. [1]

Hair-specific human data come from one small published trial and one company-reported study. In the published pilot study (Rossi and colleagues, 2013), 20 women aged 22 to 50 with acute telogen effluvium, a temporary form of shedding, were randomly assigned to a daily 2 ml scalp formulation containing 0.5% Nigella sativa oil (with glycerin, lavender oil and alcohol) or a matching placebo for three months, with follow-up at six months. [18] At three months, 9 of 10 treated women had higher hair counts versus 3 of 10 on placebo; cumulative hair thickness rose in all treated women; signs of peripilar inflammation resolved in the treated group; and three dermatologists rating photographs scored 7 treated women improved and 3 stable. The authors reported significant improvement in 70% of treated patients and no adverse effects, and described the work as a small pilot. [18] A trade-press report from September 2026 describes a study sponsored by TriNutra of a scalp lotion with 5% of its cold-pressed black seed oil (3% thymoquinone) in 22 adults over 28 days, reporting a 35% reduction in hair loss and a 7% increase in hair density; the report names no journal, and the company released the results. [19] No trial has tested black seed oil taken orally, or in androgenetic alopecia.

Registered and published human trials of black seed oil examine other conditions. A systematic review of osteoarthritis pooled six randomized trials with 370 knee osteoarthritis patients [9], and individual trials have examined knee osteoarthritis pain [10], asthma control [11], seasonal allergy [12], metabolic measures in coronary artery disease [13] and polycystic ovary syndrome [14]. Registered trials list conditions including type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, ADHD and stress. One randomized open-label trial studied the oil in mild COVID-19 [15].

Laboratory research on thymoquinone is extensive and has focused largely on cancer cell lines and animal models [7]. Wikipedia's thymoquinone page notes that the compound is classed as a pan-assay interference compound, meaning it can act on many proteins in screening assays, and that its biological properties remain under basic research [16].

In the United States the FDA classifies the plant as Generally Recognized as Safe for use as a spice or flavoring, which concerns culinary amounts [1]. Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis from thymoquinone-containing topical products, including one called Prostaquinon [17].

card.summary: Nigella sativa oil promoted for hair, with research on it centred on other conditions and none found on hair.
card.aka: Nigella sativa oil, black cumin oil, kalonji oil

quick.overview:
Black seed oil comes from Nigella sativa seeds and has a long folk-medicine history. Some people use it for hair growth or thickness.
There are no hair studies; the research on it covers other conditions and laboratory work on thymoquinone.
quick.mechanism: Its main active compound is thymoquinone, studied mostly for anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects in the lab. A hair mechanism has not been established.
quick.risks: The FDA classifies the plant as generally recognized as safe as a spice or flavoring; this concerns food use, and the safety of the oil on the scalp is not covered.
